text: Hi, this is Brightloop, a subscription management system built for the Odoo and FLUX Lucknow hackathon. It runs a subscription business end to end: products and plans, quotation to subscription, automatic recurring invoicing, discounts, payments, and a finance dashboard. It's a custom Node and PostgreSQL backend with a React front end, no static data, no backend-as-a-service. Everything you'll see is read from or written to a real database.

Subscriptions look simple, and aren't. You have to bill every customer, every period, never twice, never skipped. You have to apply the right discount and the right tax at the right moment. Every subscription has to move through a strict lifecycle, and your finance numbers have to stay honest in real time. Brightloop solves all of that on a real relational database, with three things at its core: idempotent recurring billing, automatic discounts and tax, and proper role-based access.

Architecturally it's a clean three-tier app. The React single-page app calls the API with a JWT in the header. The Express API runs every request through the same pipeline: authenticate, check the role, validate the body with Zod, then a thin route hands off to a transactional service, which calls pure domain rules. Those domain rules and the invoice maths are unit-tested with no database at all. And PostgreSQL does the heavy lifting: parameterised SQL everywhere, row locks where it matters, and SQL views that feed the dashboard. Business logic never leaks into the routes.

Let's log in as admin and set up the catalogue. Products can carry variants. Here a Brand equals Odoo variant adds five hundred and sixty rupees to the price, so the final price becomes two thousand five hundred sixty. Plans set the billing cadence: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, along with per-plan flags like auto-close and pause that decide what's legal later. And I've armed a discount: ten percent off for five or more seats. I don't apply it by hand. It attaches itself to the next invoice automatically, and stops the moment it expires or runs out.

Now a subscription. I create it from a quotation template, so the plan and the line items come in automatically with a live price preview, then I pick a customer. Watch the status move: Draft, Quotation, Confirmed, Active. The important part is that the buttons only ever offer the legal next state. This is a real state machine enforced on the server. If you try an illegal transition, the API returns a 409. The UI isn't just hiding buttons; the database-backed rules won't allow it.

This is the signature moment. I hit Run Billing. The system finds every active subscription that's due and creates one invoice each, four hundred twenty-nine invoices, with the discount and the tax already applied. Now watch what happens when I run it again. Zero invoices created. Four hundred twenty-nine periods skipped. Nothing is billed twice, ever. And that guarantee isn't in the app code, it's in the database: a unique constraint on subscription and period, plus insert on conflict do nothing, backed by a per-subscription row lock. Run it ten times, you still get exactly one invoice per period. Missed periods get caught up on the next run.

Payments close the loop. I open an invoice and record a part payment, fourteen hundred rupees against a balance of twenty-eight sixteen. The invoice stays Confirmed with a balance showing. Then I record the rest, and the invoice flips to Paid on its own. Paid is never a status you can just set. It's only reachable by recording real payments that cover the total. And if you try to overpay, the API rejects it with a 409.

Access control is strict, and it's three-tiered. Admin owns the catalogue and adds staff. Staff do the daily work: subscriptions, invoices, billing, payments, but can't touch admin setup. Customers only ever see their own subscriptions and invoices; hit a staff route as a customer and you get a 403. Validation is just as strict: try a weak password and you get a clear, field-level error from both the client and the server. And when I sign in as the customer, the admin screens simply aren't there, enforced by a requireRole check that re-runs on every single request, so deactivating a user cuts them off instantly.

Back as staff, the finance dashboard. KPI cards for active subscriptions, monthly recurring revenue, revenue collected, outstanding and overdue. A revenue-by-month chart, an overdue table oldest-first, and CSV export, all driven by SQL views, not computed in JavaScript. And this isn't a toy dataset: it's running over roughly five thousand seeded subscriptions and twelve thousand invoices. Every heavy list page responds in tens of milliseconds. The requirement was under two seconds.

Let me show you the running product itself. I sign in as admin at the live URL, and I'm straight into the finance dashboard. These are real numbers coming from PostgreSQL. Over to Subscriptions: every status chip you see comes from that enforced state machine. Into Invoices, and this is the one-click moment, Run Billing for today. Four hundred twenty-nine invoices created in one pass, each with tax and discount already applied; run it again and you'd get zero. Finally the customer portal. Signed in as a customer, they see only their own subscription and their own invoices, nothing else. Same codebase, deployed live on Render with a managed PostgreSQL database, behind a single public URL.

None of this is just syntax-checked, it's verified end to end against a live PostgreSQL. Forty-seven tests pass: thirty-five unit and access-control tests, twelve database-backed integration tests. Billing idempotency is proven: first run four hundred twenty-nine invoices, second run zero. Role scoping holds. Lists over five thousand rows come back in twenty to forty milliseconds. And it's deployed live on Render with its own managed PostgreSQL, behind one public URL, from the same codebase.

So that's Brightloop: a custom relational backend with real dynamic data, enforced state machines, idempotent billing, automatic discounts and tax, role-based access, and a finance dashboard, all verified end to end and running live. Thanks for watching. The live demo and admin login are on screen if you'd like to try it yourself.
